anecdote

NOUN
1. A short account of a real incident, often personal, interesting, or amusing.
She opened her presentation with an anecdote about her first programming job.

anecdotal

ADJECTIVE
1. Based on individual experiences or reports rather than systematic research or measurement.
The feedback is encouraging, but so far the evidence is anecdotal.

Everyday situations: what you can say

SituationNatural sentencesWhat to notice
You use a personal story in a presentation.She shared an anecdote about her first programming job. / She opened with an anecdotal account of her first programming job.Anecdote names the short account; anecdotal describes an account based on personal experience.
You assess feedback before drawing a broad conclusion.We have a few customer anecdotes, but the evidence is still anecdotal.Individual experiences can be accurate and useful without showing how common an outcome is.

Difference / overlap

An anecdote is a short account of a real incident; it need not be funny. Anecdotal describes stories or information based on individual experiences rather than systematic study. Anecdotal does not mean false: the limitation concerns the basis and generalizability of the evidence.

Common patterns

anecdote: tell/share/recount an anecdote; an anecdote about + person/event.
anecdotal: anecdotal evidence; anecdotal reports/accounts. Anecdotal evidence can be true without establishing a general pattern.
Synonyms
anecdote
1. story — RELATED; broader; stories may be longer or fictional.
anecdotal
1. experience-based — RELATED; a descriptive phrase; not all experience-based information has a limited evidence base.
Antonyms
anecdote
No useful antonym for this word.
anecdotal
1. systematic — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; for evidence gathered through a planned method.

column3: assure: verb · reassure: verb · guarantee: verb · noun
column6:
assure

VERB
1. Tell someone confidently that something is true or will happen.
I assured her that we could meet the deadline.

reassure

VERB
1. Make someone feel less worried or doubtful.
The doctor reassured me that the results were normal.

guarantee

VERB
1. promise or make certain that an outcome will happen.
We can't guarantee that the fix will work.
NOUN
1. a promise that something will happen or meet a standard.
There is no guarantee that the fix will work.

Everyday situations: what you can say

SituationNatural sentencesWhat to notice
You confidently address someone’s concern.“I assured her that everything was fine.” / “I reassured her that everything was fine.”Both work; reassure explicitly addresses worry or doubt.
You distinguish comfort from a promise.“I can reassure you that we’re doing our best, but I can’t guarantee success.”Guarantee commits to an outcome or certainty; reassurance need not do that.

Difference / overlap

Assure and reassure overlap when a confident statement reduces worry: “I assured/reassured her that everything was fine.” Reassure explicitly addresses worry or doubt. Guarantee is a stronger commitment to an outcome or certainty: “I can reassure you that we’re doing our best, but I can’t guarantee success.” Use assure/reassure + PERSON + that-clause; guarantee can take a that-clause directly.

Common patterns

assure: assure someone that + clause; assure someone of + noun
reassure: reassure someone that + clause; reassure someone about + issue
guarantee: guarantee that + clause; guarantee something; guarantee someone a refund; a guarantee that + clause; no guarantee of + outcome
Synonyms
assure
1. reassure — RELATED; overlaps when addressing a concern.
reassure
1. comfort — RELATED; broader emotional support.
guarantee
1. ensure — RELATED; for making certain, without necessarily making a promise.
Antonyms
assure
No useful antonym for this word.
reassure
1. worry — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE.
guarantee
No useful antonym for this word.

column5: astray. deviate. detour. get off track. go off the rails.
column6:
astray

ADVERB
1. Away from the correct path or destination.
The hikers went astray after missing a trail marker.
2. Away from the correct belief, plan, or standard of behavior.
A misleading benchmark led the engineering team astray.
3. Lost or sent to the wrong place.
My package seems to have gone astray.

deviate

VERB
1. Depart from a route, plan, rule, or expected pattern. This can be deliberate and need not be bad.
We deviated from the original plan to accommodate the client’s request.

detour

NOUN
1. An alternative or indirect route, often taken to avoid an obstacle or visit somewhere.
We took a detour because the road was closed.
VERB
1. Travel by an alternative or indirect route.
We detoured through a nearby town.

get off track

IDIOM
1. Move away from the intended topic, task, or direction.
We got off track discussing features we don’t actually need.

go off the rails

IDIOM
1. Become uncontrolled or depart badly from the intended course; informal.
The discussion went off the rails when people started trading insults.

Everyday situations: what you can say

SituationNatural sentencesWhat to notice
A discussion wanders away from its purpose.“We’re getting off track.” / “We’re deviating from the topic.”Both work. Off track is conversational; deviating sounds more formal.
You adapt a plan intentionally.“We deviated from the plan to include the new requirements.”Deviate need not mean making a mistake. Go astray would suggest something went wrong.
A road is closed.“We had to take a detour.” / “We had to deviate from our planned route.”Both describe changing routes. Take a detour is the everyday travel expression.
Bad advice takes you in the wrong direction.“That advice led me astray.” / “That advice got me off track.”Both can work. The first emphasizes being misled; the second emphasizes losing your intended direction.
A meeting becomes chaotic.“The meeting went off the rails.”Stronger than merely getting off topic; it suggests things became difficult to control.

Difference / overlap

These expressions overlap around leaving an intended direction. Get off track is an everyday default for losing focus. Deviate from describes departure from something specified, including deliberate changes. Take a detour is especially useful for an alternative route and can also describe a temporary diversion in discussion. Go astray suggests a wrong direction, an error, or something becoming lost. Go off the rails is usually a stronger, more dramatic description of things going wrong. Do not force a distinction where several choices work.

Common patterns

astray: go astray; lead someone astray. Astray is an adverb; go or lead supplies the verb.
deviate: deviate from + plan, route, rule, topic.
detour: take a detour; a detour around something; detour through somewhere.
get off track: get/go off track; get someone back on track.
go off the rails: go off the rails; a meeting/project goes off the rails. Keep the and plural rails.
Synonyms
astray
1. off course — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; also used figuratively for a plan or process.
1. in the wrong direction — RELATED; a transparent phrase with a broader grammatical range.
deviate
1. depart from — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; when the construction is adjusted.
detour
1. alternative route — RELATED; not every alternative route is indirect.
get off track
1. get sidetracked — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; for losing focus.
go off the rails
1. go wrong — RELATED; broader and less suggestive of losing control.
Antonyms
astray
1. on course — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; for direction.
deviate
1. adhere to — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; for following a plan or rule.
detour
No useful antonym for this word.
get off track
1. stay on track — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE.
go off the rails
1. stay under control — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE.

column5: compromise. meet halfway. concede. give in. back down
column6:
compromise

NOUN
1. an agreement reached by accepting less than originally wanted.
We reached a compromise on the deadline.
VERB
1. accept less than originally wanted to reach agreement.
We compromised on the deadline.
2. weaken or put something at risk.
Sharing passwords can compromise security.

meet halfway

IDIOM
1. Accept part of another person's wishes so both sides can agree.
If you can extend the deadline, I'll meet you halfway on the scope.

concede

VERB
1. Admit that something is true, or yield something after resisting.
I concede that your approach is simpler.

give in

PHRASAL VERB
1. Stop resisting and agree to a demand or temptation.
I finally gave in and agreed to help.

back down

PHRASAL VERB
1. Withdraw a position or demand after opposition.
She refused to back down on the deadline.

Everyday situations: what you can say

SituationNatural sentencesWhat to notice
Two sides adjust their demands.“We compromised on the deadline.” / “We met each other halfway on the deadline.”Both work for mutual adjustment.
Someone yields in a negotiation.“They conceded on the deadline.”Concede can mean yield something after resisting.
You acknowledge a point.“I concede that your approach is simpler.”Concede that + clause means admit a point; it need not mean accept a demand.
Someone stops resisting.“She finally gave in.” / “She finally backed down.”Often overlapping; neither requires a mutual compromise.
An action puts something at risk.“Sharing passwords compromises security.”Compromise also means weaken or endanger.

Difference / overlap

Compromise and meet someone halfway often describe the same mutual adjustment. Concede can mean admit a point or yield something. Give in and back down often overlap for stopping resistance; neither requires both sides to adjust. Compromise security means put security at risk, not negotiate.

Common patterns

compromise: reach a compromise; compromise with someone on something; compromise security
meet halfway: meet someone halfway; meet each other halfway
concede: concede that + clause; concede a point; concede defeat; make a concession (the related noun phrase). We made a concession on the deadline to reach an agreement. A concession is something you agree to give up or allow; it need not mean that both sides compromise.
give in: give in to + pressure/demand/temptation
back down: back down on/from + position/demand; refuse to back down
Synonyms
compromise
1. agreement — RELATED; for the noun.
2. meet halfway — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; for mutual adjustment.
meet halfway
1. compromise — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; in negotiation.
concede
1. admit — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; for acknowledging a fact.
2. yield — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; for giving way.
give in
1. yield — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; more formal.
back down
1. give in — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; in many disputes.
Antonyms
compromise
No useful antonym for this word.
meet halfway
No useful antonym for this word.
concede
1. deny — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; of admitting a claim.
give in
1. hold out — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; when continuing to resist.
back down
1. stand firm — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE.

column3: conquer: verb · occupy: verb · annex: verb · noun · colonize: verb
column5: to conquer. to occupy. to annex. an annex. to colonize.
column6:
conquer

VERB
1. Defeat a people or army and gain control of their land by force.
The army conquered the neighboring kingdom.
2. Successfully overcome a fear, difficulty, or other obstacle.
She conquered her fear of public speaking.

occupy

VERB
1. Fill or use a space, or hold a position.
The cabinet occupies most of the room.
2. Keep someone busy or use their time or attention.
The migration occupied most of our time that week.
3. Take or maintain control of a place, especially with armed forces.
Foreign troops occupied the city.

annex

VERB
1. Add or claim territory as part of a country, state, or city, often by taking control of it.
The empire annexed the border region.
NOUN
1. An additional building or part of a building used with a main building.
The library keeps its archives in a separate annex.
2. A supplementary section attached to a document, especially an official report or agreement.
The technical requirements are listed in an annex to the agreement.

colonize

VERB
1. Establish a colony in a place, through settlement or control by an outside population or power.
Several European powers colonized territories overseas.
2. For organisms, establish a population in a new place or habitat.
Bacteria quickly colonized the exposed surface.

Everyday situations: what you can say

SituationNatural sentencesWhat to notice
An army gains and then holds control of a city.The army conquered the city. / The army occupied the city.Both may describe the same conflict. Conquer emphasizes defeating resistance and gaining control; occupy emphasizes holding the place.
A country claims a neighboring region as part of itself.It occupied the region but did not annex it.Military control does not automatically mean incorporation into the country. Annex describes that claim or incorporation, without implying international recognition.
An outside power establishes a colony.The power conquered the territory and later colonized it.Conquer highlights military victory; colonize highlights establishing a colony through settlement or outside rule. These actions can overlap and need not occur in this order.
You describe ordinary work or personal challenges.The migration occupied most of our time. / She conquered her fear of speaking in meetings.Occupy also concerns space, roles, time, and attention. Conquer also means overcome a difficulty; annex and colonize do not normally replace them here.

Difference / overlap

All four can concern territorial control, and several may describe the same event. Conquer emphasizes gaining control through defeat; occupy emphasizes control or presence; annex emphasizes adding or claiming territory as part of a political unit; colonize emphasizes establishing a colony. They are not a fixed sequence. Annex also names a building addition or document supplement; colonize also describes organisms establishing themselves in a habitat.

Common patterns

conquer: conquer + city/territory/kingdom; conquer a fear; conquer a difficult challenge.
occupy: occupy + place/space/position; occupy most of the room; occupy a senior role. She occupies a senior position at the company. Occupy someone’s time/attention; occupy yourself with + noun/V-ing. Keep yourself occupied = keep yourself busy.
annex: annex + territory/region; annex an area to a country. Noun: an annex to a building/report; in the annex. American spelling: annex for both noun and verb.
colonize: colonize + territory/island/planet; bacteria/plants colonize a surface/habitat. Related nouns: colony; colonization.
Synonyms
conquer
1. defeat — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; for overcoming an opponent; defeat alone does not always imply taking territory.
1. overcome — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; for fears and difficulties.
occupy
1. take up — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; for space; not a substitute in every role context.
1. take up — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; for time.
2. keep busy — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; for a person; requires a different construction.
1. take control of — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; also has broader nonmilitary uses.
annex
1. incorporate — RELATED; broader; normally incorporate the territory into a larger political unit.
1. extension — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; for a building addition; an annex may also be a separate nearby building.
1. appendix — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; for supplementary document material; institutional naming practices vary.
colonize
1. settle — RELATED; overlaps in settlement contexts but does not itself imply colonial rule.
1. establish themselves in — RELATED; requires a plural subject and a different construction.
Antonyms
conquer
1. surrender to — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; for yielding to an opponent rather than overcoming it.
occupy
1. vacate — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; a space or position.
1. withdraw from — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; a territory.
annex
1. cede — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; for giving up territory to another power.
colonize
1. decolonize — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; for ending colonial rule.

Everyday situations: what you can say

SituationNatural sentencesWhat to notice

1. straightforward — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; open and honest about intentions.
NOUN
1. Skill in achieving something through clever planning or deception.
The general relied on cunning rather than brute force.
The noun is uncountable and is more common in literary or formal writing.

NOUN
1. A three-dimensional shape with two parallel circular ends and one curved surface.
The students calculated the volume of the cylinder.
A circle is two-dimensional; a cylinder is three-dimensional.
2. A container, chamber, or machine part shaped approximately like a cylinder.
The mechanic found damage inside one of the engine's cylinders.
Synonyms
No useful synonym for this word.
Antonyms
No useful antonym for this word.

ADJECTIVE
1. Distrustful of people’s sincerity, honesty, or motives.
He's cynical about the company's promises.
Common patterns: be cynical about + promise/politics/motives; a cynical attitude. Skeptical doubts a claim; cynical often questions whether people mean what they say. Both can fit a promise, with different emphasis.
Synonym
1. distrustful — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; broader; not limited to beliefs about motives.
Antonym
1. trusting — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; of people’s motives.

ADJECTIVE
1. Slightly wet; not completely wet.
The morning mist left my jacket damp.
Synonyms
1. moist — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; often more neutral or positive, especially for food, skin, and soil.
2. wet — RELATED; broader and usually indicates more water.
Antonym
1. dry — DIRECT OPPOSITE.

NOUN
1. A fault or flaw that makes something imperfect or prevents it from working properly.
The team found a defect in the authentication code.
Common patterns: defect from + organization/country; defect to + rival/competitor. Noun patterns: a defect in + product/system; a manufacturing defect.
Synonyms
1. flaw — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE.
2. fault — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE.
VERB
1. Leave one side or organization to join a rival.
Several engineers defected to a competitor.
Can imply disloyalty; changed employers is a more neutral description.
Synonym
1. switch sides — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; broader and often less judgmental.
Antonyms
No useful antonym for this word.

NOUN
1. Open, determined refusal to obey or respect someone or something.
The company continued operating in defiance of the court order.
Synonyms
1. disobedience — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; focuses more directly on failure to obey.
2. resistance — RELATED; broader and not always openly confrontational.
Antonym
1. obedience — DIRECT OPPOSITE; compliance with an order or authority.

NOUN
1. A god or goddess.
The temple was dedicated to a deity associated with the sea.
Synonyms
1. god — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; more common and less formal.
2. divine being — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; a neutral descriptive phrase.
Antonyms
No useful antonym for this word.

column3: deprive: verb · deprecate: verb · depreciate: verb
column6:
deprive

VERB
1. Take away or deny something needed, valued, or deserved.
The noise deprived us of sleep.

deprecate

VERB
1. In software, mark a feature as discouraged or no longer recommended; also formally express disapproval.
We deprecated the old endpoint in favor of the new API.
2. Express disapproval; formal and less common in everyday conversation.
The writer deprecated the use of violence.

depreciate

VERB
1. Lose monetary value; in accounting, reduce an asset's recorded value over time.
Cars usually depreciate as they get older.
2. Reduce an asset’s recorded value over time in accounting.
The company depreciates its equipment over five years.

Everyday situations: what you can say

SituationNatural sentencesWhat to notice
Noise keeps you from sleeping.“The noise deprived me of sleep.”Deprive someone of something.
An old API is no longer recommended.“We deprecated the old API.”Discouraged use; not necessarily removed.
A car loses value.“Cars depreciate as they get older.”Depreciate describes value or accounting.

Difference / overlap

These three verbs are not synonyms. Deprive means deny something needed or valued; deprecate means discourage software use or formally disapprove; depreciate concerns monetary value or accounting. “The noise deprived me of sleep.” “We deprecated the old API.” “Cars depreciate.” A deprecated feature can still work; the status does not itself mean removal.

Common patterns

deprive: deprive someone of + noun; be deprived of + noun
deprecate: deprecate an API/feature; a deprecated method
depreciate: depreciate in value; depreciate equipment over five years
Synonyms
deprive
1. deny — RELATED; deny someone something.
deprecate
1. discourage — RELATED; for software.
2. disapprove of — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; for general disapproval.
depreciate
1. lose value — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; for market value.
Antonyms
deprive
1. provide — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; provide someone with something.
deprecate
1. endorse — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; of disapproval.
depreciate
1. appreciate — DIRECT OPPOSITE; for market value.

column6:
ADJECTIVE
1. Careful about small details.
She's a detail-oriented engineer.
Common patterns: a detail-oriented + person/professional; be detail-oriented. Meticulous and detail-oriented overlap; do not force a distinction when either naturally describes careful work.
Synonym
1. meticulous — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; often emphasizes especially thorough, precise work.
Antonym
1. careless — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; in attention to detail.

ADJECTIVE
1. Completely lacking something that would normally be present.
The proposal was ambitious but devoid of practical details.
Pattern: be devoid of something.
Synonym
1. lacking — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; less emphatic and used in more grammatical patterns.
Antonym
1. full of — DIRECT OPPOSITE; used when something contains a large amount of something.

ADVERB
1. In a tactful way that avoids offending people or creating unnecessary conflict.
She diplomatically suggested that the team reconsider the timeline.
Common with respond, handle, phrase, suggest, and decline. It describes how someone communicates or manages disagreement.
Synonyms
1. tactfully — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; the closest everyday alternative.
2. carefully — RELATED; broader and does not necessarily involve avoiding offense.
Antonym
1. bluntly — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; speaks very directly, sometimes without regard for offense.
2. Through negotiation and official relations between countries rather than through force.
The two governments agreed to resolve the dispute diplomatically.
Synonym
1. through negotiation — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; states the method explicitly.
Antonym
1. militarily — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; through armed force rather than diplomacy.

VERB
1. To notice, recognize, or understand something that is difficult to perceive clearly.
Analysts struggled to discern a clear trend in the data.
Common objects include a pattern, trend, difference, shape, sound, and meaning. It is more formal than notice or make out.
Synonyms
1. detect — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; more neutral and often used for measurable or observable signs.
2. make out — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; more conversational, especially for something hard to see or hear.
3. distinguish — RELATED; especially natural when identifying a difference between things.
Antonym
1. overlook — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; fail to notice something.

NOUN
1. Spoken or written communication about a subject, especially within society or an academic field.
Social media has transformed public discourse about mental health.
Synonyms
1. discussion — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; less formal and may refer to one specific exchange.
2. dialogue — RELATED; emphasizes an exchange between participants.
3. debate — RELATED; emphasizes competing opinions or disagreement.
2. Connected language examined in its social context, especially in linguistics.
The researchers analyzed political discourse on social media.
Antonyms
No useful antonym for this word.

ADJECTIVE
1. Careful not to reveal private information or cause embarrassment.
Please be discreet when discussing the reorganization with the team.
Do not confuse discreet with discrete, which means separate and distinct.
Synonyms
1. tactful — RELATED; focuses on avoiding offense in social situations.
2. confidential — RELATED; usually describes information or a relationship, not a person's behavior generally.
Antonym
1. indiscreet — DIRECT OPPOSITE; careless about privacy or embarrassment.
2. Not likely to attract much attention; unobtrusive.
A discreet camera was mounted above the entrance.
Synonyms
1. unobtrusive — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; designed not to attract attention.
2. subtle — RELATED; broader and often describes slight effects or differences.
Antonym
1. conspicuous — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; easy to notice.

VERB
1. To force people to leave their homes or usual location.
The flooding displaced thousands of residents from coastal communities.
Synonym
1. force out — RELATED; more direct and less formal.
2. To take the position, role, or function previously held by someone or something else.
Automation may displace some routine administrative jobs.
Synonym
1. replace — RELATED; focuses on what takes the old thing's place, while displace focuses on what is removed.
3. To move something from its normal position or cause a substance to occupy a different space.
The object displaced an equal volume of water when it was submerged.
Synonym
1. move — RELATED; much broader and does not imply removal from an existing position.
Antonyms
No useful antonym for this word.

ADJECTIVE
1. Feeling as though you or your surroundings are spinning, often with a loss of balance.
I felt dizzy after standing up too quickly.
Common patterns: feel/get dizzy; make someone dizzy. Feel/get dizzy; make someone dizzy.
Synonym
1. lightheaded — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; overlaps but often emphasizes feeling faint rather than spinning.
Antonyms
No useful antonym for this word.

NOUN
1. An opening or pipe through which wastewater flows away.
The shower drain is clogged.
2. Something that gradually uses up money, energy, or another resource.
The constant meetings are a drain on my energy.
Synonym
1. burden — RELATED; emphasizes difficulty rather than resource depletion.
VERB
1. Remove liquid from something, or let liquid flow away.
Drain the pasta before adding the sauce.
2. Gradually use up strength, power, money, or another resource.
Background apps can drain the battery.
Synonym
1. deplete — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; more formal.
Antonym
1. replenish — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE.

VERB
1. To make someone or something completely wet, usually with a large amount of liquid.
The sudden downpour drenched everyone waiting for the bus.
Synonym
1. soak — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; can also mean to leave something in liquid for a period of time.
Antonyms
No useful antonym for this word.

IDIOM
1. Make someone learn or remember something through repeated, insistent instruction.
My teacher drilled that rule into us.
Common patterns: drill + rule/idea/lesson + into + person. Can sound forceful. A pronunciation drill is a practice exercise, not this instruction idiom.
Synonym
1. instill — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; can describe a slower or less repetitive process.
Antonyms
No useful antonym for this word.

PHRASAL VERB
1. Take someone or something to a place and leave them there.
We just need to drop off our bags at the airport.
Synonym
1. deliver — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; more neutral; drop off often implies a brief stop.
2. Decrease in amount or intensity.
Sales usually drop off after the holiday season.
Synonym
1. decline — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE.
Antonym
1. increase — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE.
3. Fall asleep; informal.
I dropped off as soon as the plane took off.
Synonym
1. fall asleep — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; more neutral.
Antonym
1. wake up — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE.

ADJECTIVE
1. Having a taste, smell, or color that suggests soil or the natural earth.
The mushrooms added an earthy flavor to the sauce.
2. Direct and sometimes coarse, especially in language or humor.
His earthy humor made the formal dinner less stiff.
Synonym
1. coarse — RELATED; more clearly negative.
Antonyms
No useful antonym for this word.

ADJECTIVE
1. Based on observation, experiments, or measurable evidence rather than theory alone.
We need empirical evidence to determine whether the new method actually works.
Synonyms
1. evidence-based — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; common in medicine and policy, but less natural with some research nouns.
2. observational — RELATED; specifically emphasizes evidence gathered by observation.
Antonym
1. theoretical — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; based primarily on theory rather than direct observation or testing.

VERB
1. Make certain that something happens or that a condition holds.
Automated checks help ensure that every change is tested.
Common patterns: ensure + outcome/condition; ensure that + clause; ensure consistency. Ensure consistency / ensure that tests run. Assure someone that ... addresses a person with a confident statement; ensure that ... concerns making the outcome certain.
Synonyms
1. make sure — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE.
2. guarantee — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; can overlap in making certain, but can also mean making a promise.
Antonyms
No useful antonym for this word.

entice

VERB
1. Attract someone by offering something appealing, often encouraging an action.
The discount enticed me to try the service.

induce

VERB
1. Cause a state or effect; also influence someone to act, often through an incentive. Usually more formal than cause or persuade.
The medication can induce sleep.
2. Influence someone to do something, often through an incentive; formal.
The offer induced several employees to stay.

Everyday situations: what you can say

SituationNatural sentencesWhat to notice
An appealing offer makes someone stay.“The offer enticed him to stay.” / “The offer induced him to stay.”Both work. Entice highlights appeal; induce sounds more formal.
Something causes a physical effect.“The medication can induce sleep.”Induce has a cause-an-effect sense; entice does not have this construction.

Difference / overlap

Both can describe influencing someone to act: “The offer enticed/induced him to stay.” Entice highlights an appealing offer; induce is more formal and also describes causing an effect: “The medication can induce sleep.” These are useful contexts, not mutually exclusive categories.

Common patterns

entice: entice someone to + verb; entice someone into + V-ing; entice someone with + offer
induce: induce sleep/labor; induce someone to + verb
Synonyms
entice
1. tempt — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; in appealing-offer contexts.
induce
1. cause — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; for effects.
2. persuade — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; in some action contexts.
Antonyms
entice
1. deter — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE.
induce
1. prevent — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; for effects.

column6:
NOUN
1. The accepted rules for polite behavior in society or in a particular situation.
Good video-call etiquette includes muting your microphone when you are not speaking.
Usually uncountable: good etiquette, not an etiquette.
Synonyms
1. manners — RELATED; describes how an individual behaves rather than the complete set of social rules.
2. protocol — RELATED; describes formal or official procedures, which are not necessarily about politeness.
Antonym
1. rudeness — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; behavior that violates accepted standards of politeness.

ADJECTIVE
1. Remaining useful or relevant over time, especially for content or information.
We need more evergreen documentation.
Common patterns: evergreen content/documentation/advice; keep content evergreen.
Synonym
1. timeless — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; can emphasize lasting appeal rather than practical relevance.
Antonym
1. dated — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; for content that no longer feels current.
2. Keeping green leaves throughout the year.
Evergreen trees line the path.
Antonym
1. deciduous — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; for trees that lose their leaves seasonally.
NOUN
1. A tree or plant that keeps green leaves throughout the year.
We planted an evergreen near the entrance.

VERB
1. To deliberately use force, influence, pressure, authority, or effort in order to produce an effect.
The board exerted considerable pressure on the team to release the product early.
Common objects include force, pressure, influence, control, authority, and effort.
Synonyms
1. apply — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; especially common with force and pressure, but not natural with every object that exert takes.
2. wield — RELATED; usually means to use power, authority, or influence effectively.
2. To make a strong physical or mental effort.
She had to exert herself to keep the discussion focused and productive.
This sense normally uses the reflexive pattern exert yourself.
Synonym
1. make an effort — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; more common and conversational.
Antonyms
No useful antonym for this word.

VERB
1. To make a process or action happen sooner or more efficiently.
Providing the requested logs will expedite the investigation.
Common objects include a process, request, order, shipment, approval, and investigation. It is formal; speed up is more common in conversation.
Synonyms
1. speed up — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; more common and conversational.
2. accelerate — RELATED; often describes increasing the rate of a process or change.
Antonym
1. delay — DIRECT OPPOSITE; make something happen later.

NOUN
1. A bold, skillful, or remarkable action or achievement, often used in the plural.
The documentary recounts the climber's remarkable exploits.
Synonyms
1. feat — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; emphasizes an impressive achievement.
2. achievement — RELATED; broader and more neutral.
VERB
1. To use a resource, opportunity, or capability effectively in order to gain an advantage.
The scheduler exploits parallel processing to reduce latency.
Synonyms
1. make use of — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; more neutral and does not necessarily imply maximizing the benefit.
2. leverage — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; common in business and technical contexts and emphasizes gaining an advantage.
3. capitalize on — RELATED; usually takes an opportunity or favorable situation.
Antonym
1. neglect — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; fail to make use of an available resource or opportunity.
2. To take unfair advantage of a person or weakness for one's own benefit.
The company was accused of exploiting temporary workers.
Synonyms
1. take advantage of — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; negative when its object is a person or weakness.
2. abuse — RELATED; describes broader harmful or improper treatment.
Antonym
1. protect — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; prevent someone from being harmed or unfairly used.
column7: priority::active pos::noun pos::verb domain::general domain::ielts domain::professional

column6:
VERB
1. To kill all members of a group of pests or other unwanted living things in a place.
The landlord hired a company to exterminate the termites.
Common objects include termites, rats, cockroaches, and other pests. When applied to people, exterminate describes mass killing and is extremely strong and horrifying; do not use it for an ordinary individual killing.
Synonyms
1. eradicate — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; more formal and can also apply to diseases or social problems.
2. wipe out — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; more informal and broader.
Antonym
1. preserve — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; protect a population or species from destruction.

PHRASAL VERB
1. Fail to keep pace with others or with expected progress.
I fell behind on my interview preparation while traveling.
Synonym
1. lag behind — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; often emphasizes relative progress.
Antonym
1. keep up — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE.

IDIOM
1. Fail to reach a target, standard, or expectation.
The results fell short of expectations.
Common patterns: fall short of + expectations/target/standard; fall well short of + goal. Can describe a small or large gap: fall just/well short of the target.
Synonym
1. fail to meet — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; a target or standard.
Antonym
1. exceed — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; a target or standard.

ADJECTIVE
1. Raised on a farm rather than caught in the wild, especially fish or seafood.
The menu lists both wild-caught and farm-raised salmon.
Antonym
1. wild-caught — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE.
Synonyms
No useful synonym for this word.

NOUN
1. A fixture that controls the flow of water from a pipe.
The bathroom faucet keeps dripping.
Synonym
1. tap — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; tap is the usual British term; faucet is standard in American English.
Antonyms
No useful antonym for this word.

NOUN
1. The deliberate spreading of frightening or exaggerated claims in order to influence people.
Critics accused the campaign of fearmongering about an economic collapse.
Synonyms
1. scaremongering — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; more common in British English.
2. alarmism — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; emphasizes exaggerating a danger but does not always imply deliberate manipulation.
3. scare tactics — RELATED; specific methods used to frighten people into acting in a certain way.
Antonym
1. reassurance — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; communication that reduces fear or concern.

ADVERB
1. With strong, sincere, and deeply felt emotion or belief.
She fervently believes that education should be accessible to everyone.
Often modifies verbs such as believe, hope, pray, wish, support, and oppose; it is stronger and somewhat more formal than strongly.
Synonyms
1. passionately — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; broader and sometimes more emotional.
2. earnestly — RELATED; emphasizes sincerity more than intensity.
Antonym
1. halfheartedly — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; without much enthusiasm or commitment.

ADJECTIVE
1. Relating to the duties, feelings, or behavior of a son or daughter toward a parent.
She felt a strong sense of filial duty toward her aging parents.
Synonyms
No useful synonym for this word.
Antonyms
No useful antonym for this word.

NOUN
1. Food placed inside a pastry, dumpling, sandwich, or similar item.
What’s the filling in these dumplings?
2. Material used to repair a hole in a tooth.
The dentist replaced an old filling.
ADJECTIVE
1. Making you feel that you have eaten enough.
The soup was surprisingly filling.
Synonym
1. satisfying — RELATED; describes satisfaction more broadly, not only fullness.
Antonyms
No useful antonym for this word.

NOUN
1. A custard dessert usually served with a layer of caramel sauce.
We shared a slice of caramel flan after dinner.
Synonyms
No useful synonym for this word.
Antonyms
No useful antonym for this word.

ADJECTIVE
1. Having plenty of pleasant or distinctive flavor.
The chicken was tender and flavorful.
Synonym
1. tasty — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE.
Antonym
1. bland — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE.

ADJECTIVE
1. Soft, light, and full of air.
The rice was light and fluffy.
Synonym
1. airy — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; especially for food texture.
Antonym
1. dense — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE.
2. Covered in soft hair or fibers.
She wore a fluffy sweater on the flight.
Synonym
1. fuzzy — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; often suggests fine, soft fibers.

VERB
1. To fail an exam, class, or course.
I nearly flunked my driving test.
Mainly American English and informal; fail is the neutral alternative.
Synonym
1. fail — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; more neutral and used in a wider range of contexts.
Antonym
1. pass — DIRECT OPPOSITE; succeed in an exam, class, or course.
2. To give a student a failing grade.
The professor flunked two students who had submitted no work.
Synonym
1. fail — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; more neutral.

column5: fold. fold up. fold over. fold in.
column6:
NOUN
1. A line or bent part created when one part of something is placed over another.
There was a deep fold in the fabric.
Synonyms
1. crease — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; emphasizes the visible line.
2. bend — RELATED; does not necessarily create a sharp line.
VERB
1. To bend something so that one part lies over another.
Fold the paper in half before cutting it.
Common combinations include fold clothes, fold a sheet of paper, fold something in half, and fold your arms.
Synonyms
1. bend — RELATED; broader and does not require one part to lie over another.
2. crease — RELATED; emphasizes creating a visible fold line.
Antonyms
1. unfold — DIRECT OPPOSITE; open something that has been folded.
2. flatten — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; make something level and remove its folded shape.
COMMON PHRASAL VERBS AND CONSTRUCTIONS
1. FOLD UP — to make something smaller by folding it or to move one part upward by folding.
Fold the lower-left corner up diagonally.
Separable: fold up the map, fold the map up, and fold it up; not fold up it.
Synonyms
1. collapse — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; applies to furniture or structures designed to fold.
2. compact — RELATED; make something take up less space.
Antonym
1. unfold — DIRECT OPPOSITE; return something to its open position.
2. FOLD OVER — to bend or turn one part so that it lies over another part.
Fold the top edge over by two inches.
Separable: fold the edge over and fold it over; not fold over it.
Synonyms
1. turn over — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; works in some physical instructions.
2. bend over — RELATED; may not result in one part lying flat against another.
Antonym
1. unfold — DIRECT OPPOSITE; return something to its open position.
3. FOLD IN — in cooking, to gently combine an ingredient with a mixture without removing too much air.
Gently fold the egg whites into the batter.
Synonyms
1. mix in — RELATED; broader and does not describe the gentle folding technique.
2. incorporate — RELATED; formal and does not specify how the ingredients are combined.

NOUN
1. The traditional stories, beliefs, and customs of a community or culture.
Dragons appear in the folklore of many different cultures.
Synonym
1. tradition — RELATED; broader and can include practices that are not stories or beliefs.
2. Widely repeated stories or beliefs associated with a modern group or subject, whether or not they are true.
Company folklore says the first prototype was built over a single weekend.
Synonym
1. legend — RELATED; usually refers to one particular traditional or widely repeated story.
Antonyms
No useful antonym for this word.

ADJECTIVE
1. Feeling warm affection or liking for someone or something.
I have grown fond of my teammates since joining the project.
Common pattern: be or grow fond of + noun, pronoun, or -ing form.
Synonyms
1. affectionate toward — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; emphasizes emotional warmth.
2. attached to — RELATED; suggests a stronger emotional connection.
3. partial to — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; slightly formal and often used for things or activities.
Antonyms
1. indifferent to — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; having no particular interest or affection.
2. hostile toward — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; feeling active dislike.
2. Filled with or expressing affection and pleasant feelings.
I have fond memories of working with that team.
Synonyms
1. affectionate — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; particularly natural with looks, gestures, and farewells.
2. warm — RELATED; expresses friendliness or positive emotion.
3. cherished — RELATED; emphasizes that a memory is deeply valued.
Antonym
1. painful — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; for memories, associated with distress rather than affection.

ADJECTIVE
1. Designed to be very hard to misuse or get wrong.
We need a foolproof way to avoid accidental deployments.
Common patterns: a foolproof method/plan/system; make + process/instructions + foolproof. Also: We should make the installation process foolproof. It often expresses strong confidence, not a literal guarantee that failure is impossible.
Synonym
1. reliable — RELATED; broader; does not specifically emphasize resistance to mistakes.
Antonyms
No useful antonym for this word.

VERB
1. Move liquid around the back of your throat while breathing out, making a bubbling sound.
She gargled with warm salt water.
Common patterns: gargle with + liquid; gargle with warm salt water. Rinsing your mouth washes the mouth; gargling specifically involves the back of the throat.
Synonyms
No useful synonym for this word.
Antonyms
No useful antonym for this word.

VERB
1. To obtain or attract something, especially support, attention, praise, information, or votes.
The proposal garnered broad support from the engineering team.
It normally takes an intangible result rather than an ordinary physical object.
Synonyms
1. gain — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; more common and broader.
2. attract — RELATED; natural with attention and interest, but not with every object that garner can take.
Antonym
1. lose — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; means to cease to have support, attention, or approval.

VERB
1. Estimate or assess the amount, strength, or nature of something.
It's difficult to gauge customer satisfaction.
Common patterns: gauge + reaction/interest/performance; gauge how + clause.
Synonyms
1. assess — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE.
2. estimate — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE.
2. Measure something, especially with an instrument.
The sensor gauges the pressure inside the tank.
Synonym
1. measure — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE.
NOUN
1. An instrument that measures and displays an amount or level.
The fuel gauge showed that the tank was nearly empty.
Synonym
1. meter — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; for some measuring instruments.
Antonyms
No useful antonym for this word.
column7: priority::active pos::verb pos::noun domain::general domain::ielts domain::professional

column6:
IDIOM
1. Gain an advantage or control over an opponent.
We got the upper hand during negotiations.

Everyday situations: what you can say

SituationNatural sentencesWhat to notice
You travel beyond a station.“We went past the station.” / “We passed the station.”Both work; pass takes the object directly.
You get beyond an obstacle.“We couldn’t get past the crowd.” / “I can’t get past the login screen.”Get past works for physical and other obstacles.

Difference / overlap

Go past and pass often describe the same physical movement: “We went past/passed the station.” Get past also works physically and can emphasize overcoming an obstacle: “I can’t get past the login screen.” Pass is a verb taking its object directly; past follows go/get in these frames. incentive

NOUN

2. Cause or strongly motivate an action, change, or result.

1. something that sets off a reaction or event.

VERB
1. set off a reaction or event.

stimulus

NOUN
1. Something that produces a response or encourages activity; common in scientific and economic contexts.
The policy provided a stimulus to investment.

impulse

NOUN
1. A sudden urge to act, often without planning.
I resisted the impulse to check my phone.

encouragement

NOUN
1. Support that gives someone confidence or makes them more willing to act.
Her encouragement helped me keep going.

Everyday situations: what you can say

SituationNatural sentencesWhat to notice
You explain what makes work worthwhile.“The bonus is an incentive to work harder.” / “The bonus gives me motivation to work harder.”Incentive names the encouraging benefit; motivation can describe the desire or reason it creates.
You describe a reason or determination.“What was his motive for hiding it?” / “She has the drive to finish it.”Motive fits a reason behind an action; drive fits determination. Motivation can also refer to either reasons or willingness.
Something signals or sets off an action.“That was my cue to leave.” / “Stress is a trigger for my headaches.” / “The policy provides a stimulus to investment.”Cue fits a signal; trigger fits a reaction starting; stimulus is broader and often scientific or economic.
You describe an urge or support.“I resisted the impulse to buy it.” / “Her encouragement helped me keep going.”Impulse is a sudden urge; encouragement is supportive input.

Difference / overlap

These belong to related contexts, but are not nine interchangeable words for motivation. Incentive is something that makes acting worthwhile; motive is a reason behind an action. Motivation and drive overlap for willingness or determination. A cue is a signal; a trigger sets off a reaction; stimulus is broader and common in scientific/economic discussion. An impulse is a sudden urge; encouragement is supportive input. Start with familiar combinations: incentive to work, motive for lying, motivation to study, drive to succeed, cue to leave, trigger for headaches, stimulus to investment, impulse to buy, words of encouragement.

Common patterns

incentive: an incentive to + verb; offer/provide an incentive; tax incentives
motive: a motive for + noun/V-ing; an ulterior motive
motivation: motivation to + verb; motivation for + action; lack/lose motivation
drive: the drive to + verb; a drive to succeed; go for a drive; a hard drive; drive a car; drive change
cue: a cue to + verb; take your cue from someone; visual/social cues
trigger: a trigger for + reaction; identify/avoid a trigger; trigger + alert/reaction/event
stimulus: a stimulus to + activity; respond to a stimulus; plural stimuli
impulse: an impulse to + verb; on impulse; resist an impulse
encouragement: give someone encouragement; encouragement to + verb; words of encouragement

column6:
responsible for

ADJECTIVE PHRASE
1. Having a duty, causing something, or bearing responsibility for a result.
I'm responsible for reviewing pull requests.
2. Be the cause of something.
A faulty sensor was responsible for the shutdown.
3. Bear responsibility or blame for a result.

accountable for

ADJECTIVE PHRASE
1. Responsible for actions or results and expected to explain or justify them.

answerable to

ADJECTIVE PHRASE
1. Required to explain or justify your actions to a person or organization.
The director is answerable to the board.

in charge of

PREPOSITIONAL PHRASE
1. Managing, directing, or having control over something.
Maya is in charge of the project.

Everyday situations: what you can say

SituationNatural sentencesWhat to notice
Someone must answer for mistakes.“You’ll be held responsible for mistakes.” / “You’ll be held accountable for mistakes.”Both work; no strict distinction needed.
You describe your duties.“I’m responsible for reviewing code.”Responsible for + noun/V-ing.
You name who you answer to.“I’m accountable to my manager for the release.” / “I’m answerable to my manager for the release.”To introduces the person; for introduces the result or action.
You identify the project leader.“Maya is in charge of the project.”Management; she may also be responsible and accountable.
Something causes a failure.“A sensor was responsible for the failure.”Responsible also describes causes; a sensor cannot justify its actions.

Difference / overlap

Responsible for and accountable for often mean essentially the same thing for actions or results. “You’ll be held responsible/accountable for mistakes” is natural either way. Accountable makes explaining or justifying actions more explicit. Answerable to and accountable to name who you answer to; answerable for and accountable for name what you answer for. In charge of describes management and can overlap with both responsibility and accountability. Responsible also describes causes: “A faulty sensor was responsible for the failure”; accountable would be unusual for a sensor.

Common patterns

responsible for: be responsible for + noun/V-ing; hold someone responsible for + result
accountable for: be accountable for + noun/V-ing; be accountable to + person/body; hold someone accountable
answerable to: be answerable to + person/body; be answerable for + action/result
in charge of: be in charge of + noun/V-ing; put someone in charge of something

accountable for
1. responsible for — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; in answerability contexts.

answerable to
1. accountable to — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE.

2. Bring a question, issue, or concern to someone’s attention.

arouse

VERB
1. To cause a feeling or reaction such as interest, curiosity, suspicion, concern, or anger.
The inconsistent figures aroused the auditor's suspicion.
2. To make someone sexually excited.
The scene was intended to arouse viewers.

Everyday situations: what you can say

SituationNatural sentencesWhat to notice
You describe an increase in prices.Prices rose. / The company raised its prices.Both describe an increase. Rise has no direct object; raise names the affected thing as its object and identifies a cause.
An issue comes up during a meeting.An issue arose during the review. / I raised the issue during the review.Arise describes the issue emerging; raise describes someone bringing it up for discussion.
Unusual activity causes people to become suspicious.The discrepancy raised suspicion. / The discrepancy aroused suspicion.Both work. Arouse emphasizes causing the reaction; do not force a distinction when both are natural.
You identify the source of a problem.The error arose from an incorrect assumption. / The error rate rose after the deployment.Arise from introduces a source or cause. Rise describes an increase in the error rate.

Difference / overlap

Rise means go up or increase; arise usually means happen, emerge, or result from something. These uses have no direct object. Raise means lift, increase, or bring something up and takes an object; it also has money-raising and child-rearing senses. Arouse causes a feeling or reaction and can also mean sexually excite someone. Forms: rise–rose–risen; arise–arose–arisen; raise–raised–raised; arouse–aroused–aroused. Rise and raise also have useful noun senses.

Common patterns

rise: rise to + level; rise by + amount; rise from a chair. The sun rises. No direct object in these uses. Forms: rise–rose–risen.
arise: a problem/question/opportunity arises; arise from + source/cause. The error arose from an incorrect assumption. No direct object. Forms: arise–arose–arisen.
raise: raise + object: raise your hand/prices/standards; raise a question/concern; raise awareness of a problem; raise money for a cause; raise children/animals. Forms: raise–raised–raised. Noun: get/ask for a raise = a pay increase in American English.
arouse: arouse interest/curiosity/concern/suspicion; arouse someone’s interest in something. Be aroused can also refer to sexual excitement; the object and context identify the meaning. Forms: arouse–aroused–aroused.

Everyday situations: what you can say

SituationNatural sentencesWhat to notice
You report an accusation.“Prosecutors charged him with fraud.”Charge someone with a crime; this does not establish guilt.
You report a finding of guilt.“He was convicted of fraud.”Convict someone of a crime.
You report the punishment.“The judge sentenced him to three years in prison.”Sentence someone to a punishment.
You report strong criticism.“The judge condemned his behavior.”Condemn normally expresses disapproval; the formal legal use also permits condemned to death.

Difference / overlap

Charge is an accusation; convict is a finding of guilt; sentence imposes punishment. A person can be charged without later being convicted. Condemn usually expresses strong disapproval; its formal legal sense also permits “condemned to death.” Sentence is the usual neutral verb for reporting a prison term. This comparison focuses on the legal sense of charge; its other everyday senses are outside this proposal.

DISCOURSE MARKER
1. Acknowledge an earlier point and introduce a limitation or contrasting consideration.

FIXED EXPRESSION
1. Introduce an assumed situation or illustrative example.

Everyday situations: what you can say

SituationNatural sentencesWhat to notice
You add a limitation to an earlier claim.“The tool is useful. That said, we still need to review its output.”That said qualifies the earlier point.
You introduce an assumed example.“Let’s say the server receives a thousand requests per second. How would we scale it?”Let’s say introduces an assumption; it does not itself mark contrast.

Difference / overlap

That said qualifies an earlier claim; let’s say introduces an example or assumption. “Remote work saves time. That said, it can feel isolating.” versus “Remote work saves time. Let’s say you save an hour a day—that adds up.” A reservation here means a concern or qualification, not a booking.

let’s say: let’s say + clause; let’s say + hypothetical amount. “Let’s say $500.”

let’s say
1. suppose — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; before a hypothetical clause.

that said

turn out

PHRASAL VERB
1. To happen or develop in a particular way, often with an unexpected result.
Despite the rain, the outdoor event turned out well.
2. To be finally discovered or proved to have a particular identity or quality.
The apparent network failure turned out to be a configuration error.
3. To attend an event or appear somewhere, especially as part of a group.
More than two thousand residents turned out to vote.
4. To produce or make something, especially regularly or in large quantities.

end up

PHRASAL VERB
1. Reach a final situation after a process, often unexpectedly.
We ended up working late.

Everyday situations: what you can say

SituationNatural sentencesWhat to notice
A meeting proves useful.“The meeting ended up being useful.” / “The meeting turned out to be useful.”Both work; useful frames differ.
You discover a fact.“It turned out that the server was misconfigured.”It turned out that + clause; end up does not take this frame.
You describe attendance or production.“Hundreds of people turned out.” / “The factory turns out parts.”These are other senses of turn out, not senses of end up.

Difference / overlap

For outcomes, “The meeting ended up being useful” and “The meeting turned out to be useful” both work. End up highlights the final situation; turn out highlights how it proved to be. Useful frames: end up + V-ing/adjective/place; turn out + adjective/adverb; turn out to + verb; it turns out that + clause. Turn out also has attendance and production senses, shown in its definitions.

Common patterns

turn out: turn out + adjective/adverb; turn out to + verb; it turns out that + clause; turn out for + event; turn out + product
end up: end up + V-ing/adjective; end up in/at + place

column3: vomit: verb · noun · retch: verb · regurgitate: verb · throw up: phrasal verb
column6:
vomit

VERB
1. Bring stomach contents out through the mouth.
He vomited twice during the night.
NOUN
1. Material brought out of the stomach through the mouth.
There was vomit on the floor.

retch

VERB
1. Make the straining movements of vomiting, often without bringing anything up.
The awful smell made him retch.

regurgitate

VERB
1. Bring swallowed food back up into the mouth.
The bird regurgitated food for its chicks.
2. Repeat information or ideas without properly understanding or processing them; disapproving.
He regurgitated memorized answers instead of explaining his reasoning.

throw up

PHRASAL VERB
1. Vomit; conversational.
I felt like I was going to throw up.

Everyday situations: what you can say

SituationNatural sentencesWhat to notice
You tell a friend you were sick.I threw up twice last night. / I vomited twice last night.Both are natural. Throw up is conversational; vomit is neutral and common in medical descriptions.
Your stomach contracts but nothing comes up.I kept retching, but nothing came up.Retch names the straining action. Dry heaving is retching without bringing anything up; retching can also precede vomiting.
A bird brings food back up to feed its chicks.The bird regurgitated food for its chicks.Regurgitate emphasizes bringing swallowed food back up. This can be normal feeding behavior and does not necessarily mean illness.
An answer repeats material without showing understanding.He regurgitated the documentation instead of explaining the design.This figurative sense of regurgitate is critical. Vomit, retch, and throw up do not have this ordinary information-repetition sense.

Difference / overlap

Vomit and throw up overlap closely for bringing stomach contents out through the mouth; their main everyday difference is register. Retch emphasizes the movements or effort, often without expelling anything. Regurgitate emphasizes food returning to the mouth and also has a useful disapproving sense for repeating information without understanding or processing it. Retch is mainly a recognition target here.

Common patterns

vomit: vomit; vomit blood; feel like vomiting. Vomit is also an uncountable noun for what comes up.
retch: retch; start/keep retching; make someone retch. Usually used without a direct object.
regurgitate: regurgitate + food; regurgitate facts/ideas/memorized answers. The figurative sense usually criticizes unthinking repetition.
throw up: throw up; throw up your food; throw it up. Use threw up for the past tense and thrown up after have/has.
Synonyms

1. throw-up — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; informal noun; written with a hyphen.
retch
1. dry-heave — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; specifically when nothing is expelled.
regurgitate
1. bring back up — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; a descriptive phrase; regurgitation need not involve illness.
1. parrot — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; also critical of repeating without independent thought.
throw up
1. vomit — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; more neutral; common in medical contexts.
Antonyms
vomit

retch

Everyday situations: what you can say

SituationNatural sentencesWhat to notice
You evaluate a proposal.Her proposal is well thought out. / Her proposal is thought-provoking.The first praises the care in developing it; the second describes how it makes the audience think. Both can be true.

Both can positively describe ideas or material. Well-thought-out concerns careful development; thought-provoking concerns intellectual effect. A proposal can be both, and neither quality guarantees the other.
